Numbers and units: feet, yards, gauges, shot sizes

Lead first. British and American coaches give lead in feet or yards: “give it three feet”, “a yard in front”. This is a picture (the gap the shooter should see at the shot), not a measurement. Keep the unit as said and do not convert it in the middle of an instruction. More on lead words: How coaches say lead, and how to translate it.

Distances to targets are another matter. “It’s about thirty yards” can become “about 27 metres”, because a yard is about 0.9 m. Keep the word “about”. Directions often come as a clock face laid over the field: straight ahead is 12, so “pick it up at eleven o’clock” means slightly left. Keep the clock; do not turn it into degrees.

The gauge works backwards. A “12-bore” or “12 gauge” is not 12 mm: the smaller the number, the wider the barrel, so a 20 gauge is narrower. Both FITASC rulebooks (Chapter 7 · Permitted shotguns, Chapter 18 · Which guns are allowed) allow guns no larger than 12 gauge, with barrels at least 66 cm (26 in) long. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the line on the vest is 25 cm below the shoulder axis; British shooters may call that just under ten inches. The shoulder axis is an imaginary line across both shoulders.

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 7 · Permitted shotguns

Cartridges: both rulebooks allow a load of at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated). That is close to the “one-ounce load” British shooters talk about, because one ounce is about 28.3 g. The shot must be round pellets of one size, 2.0 to 2.5 mm across (±0.1 mm). Shot numbers differ between countries. A No. 9 is about 2 mm almost everywhere, but other numbers vary slightly between British, American and continental systems. When it matters, ask for millimetres (Shot size).

Where this is in the rules: Chapter 7 · Cartridge rules

Chokes (the narrowing at the muzzle end of the barrel) may come as names, fractions or “thou” (thousandths of an inch). Translate them in the system the coach used, and do not convert one system into another.

Key points

  • Lead in feet is a picture: keep the unit, do not convert mid-instruction
  • Target distance: yards may become “about … metres”
  • Clock face for directions: 12 = straight ahead
  • 12 gauge ≠ 12 mm; FITASC max calibre 12, barrels ≥ 66 cm (26 in)
  • 28 g ≈ one ounce; shot 2.0–2.5 mm; shot numbers differ by country — ask for mm
Stand Talk

  • Coach Give it three feet.

    Meaning: The lead picture the coach wants; a perceived gap, not a measured distance.

  • Coach Half that.

    Meaning: Use half of the previous lead.

  • Coach Pick it up at eleven o’clock.

    Meaning: Look for the target slightly left of straight ahead.

  • Coach It’s about forty yards out.

    Meaning: The target is roughly 37 metres away.

  • Coach Put a nine in the bottom barrel.

    Meaning: Put a No. 9 shot cartridge (about 2 mm) in the lower barrel, which usually fires first.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. The coach says “It’s about thirty yards.” How can you pass it on to a shooter who thinks in metres?

    1. “About 27 metres”
    2. “Exactly 27.43 metres”
    3. “About 33 metres”
    4. “About 3 metres”
    Answer

    “About 27 metres”

    A yard is a little less than a metre (about 0.9 m), so thirty yards is about 27 m. Keep “about”: the coach’s number is an estimate.

  2. What is the largest calibre allowed in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting?

    1. 10
    2. 16
    3. 20
    4. 12
    Answer

    12

    Both rulebooks allow calibre 12 at most; a smaller gauge number means a wider bore, so 10 is not allowed.

    Chapter 7 · Permitted shotguns

  3. A British guest asks whether his “one-ounce” cartridges are legal at a FITASC event. What do you know?

    1. Up to 36 g, about 1¼ ounces
    2. Any load: there is no limit
    3. A 28 g load (+2%), about one ounce
    4. Only 24 g loads are allowed
    Answer

    A 28 g load (+2%), about one ounce

    The rules allow a load of up to 28 g with a +2% tolerance, and one ounce is about 28.3 g. The shot size (2.0–2.5 mm) must also fit.
